title: "Sharing and reproducibility"

A Pixi project records everything it needs, including R itself, in two files. Share those, and anyone can recreate the environment.

## What to commit

- **Commit `pixi.toml`**: the packages you asked for, with any version constraints.
- **Commit `pixi.lock`**: the exact version of every package, including the ones they depend on, for every platform the project supports.
- **Don't commit `.pixi/`**: the installed environment. `pixi init` (and so `use_pixi()`) adds it to `.gitignore`.

## Recreate the environment

On another computer, install Pixi, get the project, and run either:

```sh
pixi install
pixi run R
```

`pixi install` only installs the environment. `pixi run R` installs it if needed, then starts R.

If `pixi.toml` has changed since `pixi.lock` was written, Pixi updates the lock file first. To install exactly what's in the lock file instead, use `pixi install --frozen`. Or use `pixi install --locked`, which stops if the lock file is out of date.

## Platforms

`pixi.lock` covers every platform listed in `pixi.toml`, under `platforms`. A new project lists only the platform it was created on. Add the platforms your collaborators use:

```sh
pixi workspace platform add linux-64 osx-arm64 osx-64 win-64
```

Every package then has to be available for all of them, which is worth knowing before a collaborator finds out.

## Updating packages

Packages stay at the versions in `pixi.lock` until you update them:

```sh
pixi update
```

This updates to the newest versions `pixi.toml` allows. `pixi upgrade` also raises the version constraints in `pixi.toml`.

## Packages as of a date

Pixi can leave out every package published after a date, so a project gets packages as they were on that day. That's useful to rerun an old analysis with the versions it was written for, without its lock file, or to check that a package still works with what users had a year ago. Set the date when you create the project, so R and every package you add are as of that day:

```r
use_pixi(date = "2025-06-01")
```

In an existing project, `pixi_set_date()` sets it and updates `pixi.lock` to match. That fails when the project pins versions newer than the date, which `pixi_add()` does for what it adds; `pixi.toml` is then left as it was.

A duration leaves out only the newest releases, e.g. those from the last week, in case one turns out to be broken or compromised:

```r
pixi_set_date("7d")
```

Only packages that were on conda-forge at the time are available. The date applies to Pixi's build backend as well, so packages built from source (`pixi_add("github::...")`) need a date after the backend's release, or a duration. `pixi_set_date(NULL)` removes the date.

## Tasks

Save the commands that run the project as tasks in `pixi.toml`, so collaborators run them the same way:

```r
rpix::pixi_add_task("analysis", "Rscript analysis.R", description = "Run the analysis")
rpix::pixi_add_task("report", "quarto render report.qmd", depends_on = "analysis")
```

Then anyone can run them, from a terminal with `pixi run report`, or from R:

```r
rpix::pixi_run("report")
```

`report` runs `analysis` first. `pixi_tasks()` lists a project's tasks.

## Continuous integration

`use_pixi_github_action()` writes a GitHub Actions workflow that installs the project's environments exactly as `pixi.lock` records them, with the [setup-pixi](https://github.com/prefix-dev/setup-pixi) action, so CI runs with the same R and packages as your computer:

```r
use_pixi_github_action("task", task = "report")   # run a Pixi task, e.g. render a report
use_pixi_github_action("check")                   # R CMD check, for a package
```

For a package, `"check"` runs r-lib's `check-r-package` on Linux, macOS and Windows (those of the project's platforms), and takes several environments, e.g. those from `use_pixi_check_matrix()`, including the `minimum` one. `"test-coverage"` and `"pkgdown"` do what r-lib's workflows of the same name do. Pixi is pinned to the version you have, and the run fails if `pixi.lock` is out of date with `pixi.toml`, so commit both.
